title: A contact path for a logistics company
excerpt: Tell the operator what happens after they request a quote, how fast you reply, and which facts to have ready. A ten-field form loses the load while it is still on the dock.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table, a handful of doors where a quote path should be one clear door.
caption: A smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a logistics quote page say above the form?
faqs.answer: Say who reads the note, what a reply contains, and the window you can keep. List the shipment facts to have ready, and state any rule that gets an instant no. A headline about partnership does not tell an operator whether a rate is coming back today.

faqs.question: How long should the first quote form be?
faqs.answer: Ask for the load: origin, destination, ready date, weight or piece count, a description, and how to reply. That is a short form, not a survey of company size and budget. Ask for credit applications and portal setup after there is a rate they might accept. Extra dropdowns on a phone are where quotes die.

faqs.question: Should claims and quotes share one form?
faqs.answer: No. A quote, a claim, a tracking problem, and a driver application are different jobs, even if one person reads the inbox. Label them the way the navigation does, and publish a window for each. One textarea will bury a time-sensitive load under a note that could have waited.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The logistics company contact page should tell an operator what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is to request a quote. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them while the freight is still waiting on a dock.

This page is not a general inbox dressed up as a relationship. The operator already knows the load. The path should take those facts and say when a number, or a no, comes back.

## Say what happens next

Write the sequence above the fields, in three lines. They send the facts. A named desk reads them. They get a rate with assumptions, a question, or a refusal. If the founder still prices the odd load, say so. If a coordinator prices standard lanes and a different person prices project freight, say which path is which.

The sequence has to match the about page and the services page. A form that says "a specialist will be in touch" while the about page names a same-day quote is two companies. Publish the true sequence in both places.

Say what a usable reply looks like. A rate, an expiration, and the assumptions: dock to dock, the weight they sent, no liftgate. Or a no, with the reason, so they can call the next carrier before the cutoff. A vague "thanks, we got it" makes people tender the same load twice and trust you less the second time.

Say what silence means. If no reply inside the window means they should call a named number, publish the number and the hours. A form that vanishes into a queue, with no rule, trains people to fax the old way, which is a clue that the page lost.

## Say how fast, and keep it

Publish a window you can meet on a bad week. Same day for standard lanes in before a named cutoff. Next morning for a mode you run less often. "As soon as possible" is not a window. Operators have heard it from desks that never wrote back, and they will not wait to find out if you are different.

When the window slips, change the sentence before you defend it. A page that still says "within two hours" while the board is at a day is a false ad on the screen where money is about to move. Update the page. Then clear the queue. The sentence is part of the operation, not a brand line.

Speed includes the page. A quote screen that waits on a heavy script before the fields can be typed will lose the person standing next to a truck. The form should work when the HTML arrives. Maps, chat, and decoration can wait, or they can stay off this URL.

Nielsen Norman Group's work on short visits is the reason the first screen cannot be a stock container and a headline about partnership. People often leave in 10 to 20 seconds when the value is unclear. Lead with the window and the list of facts. The picture, if you need one, can be small and specific. It cannot be the argument.

## What they should have ready

Put the list before the fields so the form is not a quiz.

Origin and destination. Ready date and hours. Weight and piece count, or dimensions if the freight is awkward. What it is, in a description a rater can class. Dock or no dock. A reference they will recognize on the reply.

That list is the job. It is not ten fields of company theater. Annual volume, "tell us about your supply chain," a dropdown of industries, a budget, and a timeline belong in a CRM dream. The operator has a load. Ask for the load.

Leave insurance certificates, a portal setup, and a credit application for after you have a rate they might accept. Asking for a credit packet from someone you may refuse wastes their afternoon and stores data you do not need yet.

If a rule will get an instant no, state it beside the list. No households. No hazmat. No freight into a state you do not serve. A fast no is a courtesy. A form that pretends every load is welcome, followed by a template rejection, is how you become a story at someone else's dock.

## A short form

The fields are the list, and almost nothing else. Name, a way to reach them, and the shipment facts. Four to six inputs cover a standard quote if each input is the right fact. A notes box can hold the awkward part: "receiver takes freight only before 10." Do not make the notes box do the work of a missing structured field you actually need, and do not add fields you will not read.

The W3C WCAG principles ask for understandable forms: visible labels, instructions, and errors in text. Placeholder text that disappears is not a label. A red border with no words is not an error. Say which fact is missing, next to the field, in language a coordinator uses. "Need a weight" is clearer than "This field is required."

Do not ask them to pick a persona if the button they tapped already said request a quote. A hidden value can mark the path. A second question that says "I am a shipper / carrier / partner" tells them the last page was not listening.

On a phone, each extra dropdown is a place to abandon the quote. Test the form with a thumb, outdoors. If it takes longer than telling the facts to a person, the form is too long, even if a spreadsheet of "lead fields" wanted all of them.

## Separate the other notes

Claims, tracking problems, driver applications, and partnership pitches should not land in the quote form. Give each a label that matches the navigation. "Start a claim." "Track a shipment." "Apply as a driver." They can reach one inbox with a subject line that names the job. The page still has to stop treating a quote and a lost POD as the same note.

Put a window on each path, because the windows differ. Quotes on the clock you publish. Safety issues the same day. Careers when you are hiring, and a sentence that says when you are not. Do not let a partnership form outrank the quote in size or color. The operator with freight is the reason this path exists.

If one person reads everything, the page can still show the split. You do not need three departments. You need three first sentences so the reader of the inbox knows which hat to wear. A quote buried under a vendor pitch will miss the cutoff, and the operator will be right to blame the site.

Publish a phone number only if a person answers it during the hours you print. A number that rings to a void is worse than a form with a kept window. If the operation is the form, commit to the form. Do not add a number "for a human touch" that nobody owns.

## Confirmation and the record

After they submit, repeat what happens next and the window. Send a copy to them if you can do it without enrolling them in a newsletter. The confirmation is part of the promise. A blank thank-you makes people unsure the form worked, so they send the load again and your desk prices it twice.

Restate the assumptions you captured. "We have eight pallets, Chicago to Atlanta, ready Tuesday, dock on both ends." If they see a wrong weight on that screen, they can correct it before you rate the wrong freight. A confirmation that only says "thanks" throws away that check.

Keep the promise that was on the page the day they wrote. If you tighten the cutoff later, loads already in the queue are still under the old sentence. Honor it or write to them. The contact path is an operation. Restyling the button does not retire the clock you published.

## Review the path the way the desk will feel it

Submit a quote from a phone, with a realistic load, then wait the window you printed. Read the confirmation as if the freight had to leave tomorrow. If you cannot tell whether a rate is coming, you will not be calmer than your shippers.

Open the note that arrived. The origin, the weight, the ready date, and the awkward sentence should be visible without a hunt through hidden fields. If the rater has to open five tools to understand a short form, the path is still too clever. Fix the note before you add a field.

Once a month, compare the page's clock with the actual replies, including the nos. If the gap is longer than the window, fix the desk or fix the sentence. Leaving "same day" because it sounds better is how a quote page becomes fiction, and fiction is expensive in this business because the operator has another carrier's number already open.

A clear quote path still fails if the rest of the site performs a costume. The cuts are in [what not to put on the site for a logistics company](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-logistics-company).
